interview.question: How does useSelector decide whether to re-render?
interview.answer: useSelector subscribes the component to the Redux store, runs the selector against the state, and returns the selected value. After an action is dispatched, React Redux compares the new selector result with the previous result using strict === reference equality; a different reference causes a re-render.
interview.followUp: What happens if the selector returns a new object on every call? It appears changed on every dispatch, so the component can re-render unnecessarily; memoization or an appropriate equality function can avoid that.

interview.question: How can equality behavior be changed?
interview.answer: By default, useSelector uses strict reference equality rather than shallow equality. If the selector returns a flat object of primitive fields, shallowEqual can be supplied as the equality function, either directly or through the options object.
interview.followUp: When is memoization preferable to shallowEqual? Use memoization when deriving data so the selector returns a stable cached reference until its inputs change.

interview.question: What does the selector receive, and how can useSelector be typed?
interview.answer: The selector receives the complete Redux state and should return the specific data needed by the component. Its return type is inferred from the selector's return type when the state parameter is typed; applications can also create pre-typed hooks with .withTypes().
interview.followUp: Why should selectors be typed centrally? A pre-typed hook preserves the application's RootState and dispatch types across components without repeating those definitions.

keyPoints: The default equality rule compares the previous and current selector results with strict === reference equality.
A changed selector result reference causes the component to re-render.
An unchanged selector result reference does not trigger a re-render from that store update.
Pass shallowEqual when a selector returns a suitable flat object and field-level comparison is more appropriate than one reference comparison.
gotchas: Avoid constructing a new object or array on every selector call: strict reference comparison treats each new reference as changed and can cause re-renders after unrelated dispatches.
Reducers must return new references for changed data. Mutating an existing object and returning it can leave the selector result at the same reference, so the component may not update.

Redux core::Actions and action creators.sourceTitle: Redux Fundamentals, Part 7: Standard Redux Patterns
Redux core::Actions and action creators.summary: Actions are plain objects that describe events in an application, while action creators are functions that construct those objects. Use creators to consistently prepare payloads and centralize reusable creation logic.
Redux core::Actions and action creators.explanation: An action is a plain object describing an event, typically identified by a type and carrying data in payload. An action creator is a function that constructs such an object, making its shape and any preparation logic reusable; call it and pass the result to dispatch.

example.title: Create and dispatch an action
example.explanation: The creator prepares a serializable payload, returns an action object, and the caller dispatches that object.

useCases.title: Centralize action structure
useCases.scenario: Several callers need to produce the same event shape.

useCases.title: Prepare payloads
useCases.scenario: Inputs require formatting or validation before dispatch.

useCases.title: Encapsulate creation logic
useCases.scenario: Action creation includes reusable work or asynchronous logic.

interview.question: What are actions and action creators?
interview.answer: An action is a plain object that describes what happened. An action creator is a function that creates and returns such an object, usually so callers do not repeat its shape.
interview.followUp: Why centralize creation? It provides one place to prepare data and keeps every instance of the action consistent.

interview.question: How are action creators used?
interview.answer: Call the creator to obtain an action object, then pass that result directly to dispatch. The creator can format the payload or perform preparation work before dispatch.
interview.followUp: What if preparation is asynchronous? Extract the logic into a reusable creator, commonly using thunk middleware for more complex asynchronous behavior.

interview.question: When should action creators be used?
interview.answer: Redux does not require action creators; an action object may be written inline. They are useful when an action needs preparation, additional logic, consistency, or a reusable definition.
interview.followUp: What is the modern preferred approach? Define reducers with createSlice so Redux Toolkit generates the action types and creators automatically.

keyPoints: Actions represent events rather than commands, and their data should be carried in a predictable serializable shape.
The creator's return value is the action that can be dispatched.
A creator can turn caller inputs into the payload structure expected by reducers.
Centralizing preparation avoids duplicating event-construction logic across components.
The normal flow is to invoke the creator before dispatching.
Dispatch receives the object returned by the creator.

Redux core::combineReducers.summary: Compose independently owned slice reducers into one reducer whose state is a plain object keyed by the supplied reducer names. Each dispatched action is passed to every slice reducer.
Redux core::combineReducers.explanation: Pass an object of slice reducers to produce one reducer for a plain object state tree. For each dispatched action, the result invokes every slice reducer with its own current slice and the action, then assembles those results under the supplied keys.

parameters.name: reducers
parameters.description: An object whose values are different slice reducer functions to combine.

Redux core::combineReducers.returns: A reducer function that calls the supplied reducers and constructs a state object with the same shape as the input object.

example.title: Combining independent slice reducers
example.code:
import { createStore, combineReducers } from 'redux'

const counter = (state = 0, action) =>
  action.type === 'increment' ? state + 1 : state

const todos = (state = [], action) =>
  action.type === 'add' ? [...state, action.text] : state

const rootReducer = combineReducers({ counter, todos })
const store = createStore(rootReducer)

store.dispatch({ type: 'increment' })
store.dispatch({ type: 'add', text: 'Read Redux docs' })

console.log(store.getState())
example.explanation: The combined reducer keeps counter and todos under matching root-state keys and lets each slice respond independently to dispatched actions.

useCases.title: Assemble a root reducer from domain slices
useCases.scenario: A store has separate domains such as counters, todos, or filters, each with its own reducer.

useCases.title: Compose reducers at multiple levels
useCases.scenario: A nested part of the state needs the same keyed reducer composition as the root.

useCases.title: Build a root reducer directly
useCases.scenario: The root reducer must be constructed manually rather than generated by Redux Toolkit's store setup.

interview.question: What does combineReducers do?
interview.answer: combineReducers takes an object whose values are slice reducers and returns one reducer. On each action, that reducer invokes every slice reducer and builds a state object with the same key shape.
interview.followUp: What determines the root-state names? The keys of the object passed to combineReducers, independently of the reducer variable names.

interview.question: How are actions processed across slices?
interview.answer: Each input reducer owns one state slice. The combined reducer passes that slice and the dispatched action to the corresponding reducer, then places the returned value under that reducer's key.
interview.followUp: Can multiple slices respond to one action? Yes; every slice reducer is called for every dispatched action, so several slices may update independently.

interview.question: What limitations does combineReducers have?
interview.answer: It is designed for a plain JavaScript object state tree with one reducer per slice. It does not provide arbitrary sibling state to a slice reducer or control special ordering between slice-reducer calls.
interview.followUp: What should be considered when this pattern is insufficient? Use a custom root reducer or another composition approach when cross-slice coordination, extra arguments, or call ordering is required.

keyPoints: It converts a keyed collection of slice reducers into one reducer suitable for supplying to a Redux store.
Every dispatched action is offered to every registered slice reducer rather than being routed to only one reducer.
Separate reducer functions can be maintained independently while the combined reducer coordinates their participation.
Choose the object keys deliberately to design the public shape of the root state.
The reducers argument is a keyed object whose values are the functions to compose.
The return value preserves the input object's key structure in the produced state.
gotchas: The keys in the input object determine the corresponding names in the combined state, so changing a key changes the root-state shape.

Redux core::dispatch and subscribe.summary: Redux delivers actions through `dispatch`, which synchronously runs the reducer and commits its returned state. `subscribe` registers listeners that can read the committed state with `getState()`, and returns a function for unsubscribing.
Redux core::dispatch and subscribe.explanation: `dispatch(action)` synchronously gives an action to the reducer, stores the reducer's returned state, and then notifies listeners. `subscribe(listener)` registers a callback for dispatches that may change state; the callback can call `getState()`, and the returned function removes the subscription.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: The action passed to the store; dispatch sends it to the reducer.

parameters.name: listener
parameters.description: A callback registered to observe store changes.

Redux core::dispatch and subscribe.returns: dispatch(action) returns the dispatched action; subscribe(listener) returns an unsubscribe function.

example.title: Dispatch and observe a state change
example.explanation: Registers a listener, dispatches an action, reads the committed state, then removes the listener.

useCases.title: Deliver an action
useCases.scenario: Update application state in response to a user interaction.

useCases.title: Render from subscriptions
useCases.scenario: Refresh a non-React UI after the store commits new state.

useCases.title: Bridge external consumers
useCases.scenario: Integrate Redux state changes with an external observable or service.

keyPoints: The store's base state-changing operation is `dispatch(action)`.
Dispatch invokes the reducer synchronously with the current state and action.
The reducer's returned value becomes the store's next state.
After storing the new state, Redux immediately notifies subscribed listeners.
A subscriber runs after dispatches when state might have changed; the callback itself receives no state argument.
Subscribers should call `getState()` inside the callback to read the latest store state.
Calling the function returned by `subscribe` removes that listener.
gotchas: A subscription may dispatch, but only in response to a user action or a narrowly defined condition to avoid dispatch loops.
Changes to subscriptions during an in-progress dispatch do not alter that dispatch's listener snapshot.
Do not dispatch from a reducer; reducers must remain free of side effects.

Redux core::Immutable update patterns.summary: Immutable updates copy every nesting level on the path to changed data and preserve references for unaffected branches. Redux Toolkit uses Immer to produce these updates from mutating-looking reducer code.
Redux core::Immutable update patterns.explanation: For a manual immutable update, create new objects or arrays along the path being changed, while reusing branches that are unaffected. This preserves the original state and lets Redux detect changes through reference comparisons. Redux Toolkit reducers can instead use Immer-backed mutating syntax, which produces the immutable result automatically.
Redux core::Immutable update patterns.returns: A new state value containing copied references along changed paths while retaining references for unchanged data.

example.title: Copy each changed nesting level
example.explanation: The reducer copies every object along the path to the changed value. The unrelated branch is reused, so its reference remains unchanged.

useCases.title: Deeply nested updates
useCases.scenario: A reducer changes a property inside nested objects or arrays without mutating prior state.

useCases.title: Efficient change detection
useCases.scenario: Selectors or connected components rely on reference comparisons to identify changed data.

useCases.title: Immer-backed reducers
useCases.scenario: A Redux Toolkit case reducer needs concise update logic while retaining immutable results.

interview.question: How do you manually update a deeply nested value immutably?
interview.answer: A reducer should return a new object for each nesting level that contains the changed value, while reusing unaffected branches. This preserves immutability and makes reference-based change detection effective.
interview.followUp: What happens if an unchanged nested object is copied anyway? It is still immutable, but its new reference can cause unnecessary updates for consumers that compare references.

interview.question: What rule prevents accidental mutation during immutable updates?
interview.answer: The original state must not be changed in memory. Construct the result from copies, usually with object spread and non-mutating array methods, and return that result from the reducer.
interview.followUp: Why can a shallow top-level copy be insufficient? Nested objects remain shared, so changing one through the new top-level object would also mutate the old state.

interview.question: How does Redux Toolkit simplify immutable updates?
interview.answer: Redux Toolkit's createSlice and createReducer use Immer internally. Their case reducers may use mutating-looking draft syntax, and Immer returns a safely immutable updated value.
interview.followUp: Where is that syntax unsafe? It is unsafe in ordinary hand-written reducers and other application code unless the code is running inside Immer's produce.

keyPoints: For a nested change, copy each object or array from the root down to the changed value.
Immer preserves the same path-copying behavior automatically: changed levels receive new references, while untouched levels can be reused.
Manual updates may modify a newly created copy, provided the original state and its shared references are never changed.
Redux Toolkit's createSlice and createReducer provide Immer-backed case reducers, so immutable update bookkeeping is handled for you.
gotchas: When updating nested data by hand, copying only the deepest object is insufficient; copy every containing level on the changed path.
Never mutate the existing state object or any object obtained from it; updates must leave the original reference untouched.
Mutating-style code is safe only in Redux Toolkit's Immer-enabled reducers or an explicit Immer produce callback, not in ordinary reducers.

Redux core::Pure reducers.sourceTitle: Redux Essentials, Part 1: Redux Overview and Concepts
Redux core::Pure reducers.summary: Pure reducers calculate the next Redux state from the current state and an action. They must avoid mutation, randomness, asynchronous work, and other side effects.
Redux core::Pure reducers.explanation: A pure reducer receives the previous state and an action, determines whether that action requires an update, and returns the next state. It must derive its result only from those arguments, avoid changing existing state, and perform no asynchronous work, randomness, API calls, or other side effects.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The current or previous state value.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: An action object describing what happened.

Redux core::Pure reducers.returns: The next state value; for an unrelated action, the existing state unchanged.

example.title: A pure counter reducer
example.explanation: This reducer returns a new state value for a recognized action and the existing state for every other action.

useCases.title: State transitions
useCases.scenario: Handle an action that changes one state value.

useCases.title: Action filtering
useCases.scenario: Return the current state for actions owned by other reducers.

useCases.title: Reducer composition
useCases.scenario: Compose smaller reducers to manage separate state slices.

useCases.title: Deterministic state history
useCases.scenario: Support predictable testing and time-travel debugging.

keyPoints: A reducer maps the current state and action to the next state.
The result should depend only on the reducer's two inputs.
State updates must be immutable.
Purity excludes asynchronous operations, randomness, and side effects.
First determine whether the action belongs to this reducer.
For unrelated actions, return the current state unchanged.
gotchas: Do not mutate the current state in place; create and return an immutable update instead.
Do not perform asynchronous work, calculate random values, or cause side effects inside a reducer.
Nested objects that change must also be copied rather than mutated in place.

Redux core::Single state tree.summary: Redux keeps global application state in one object tree managed by a single store. Organize that tree around domain data and app state, then update it through actions handled by reducers.
Redux core::Single state tree.explanation: Redux keeps the application’s shared state in one store as a single state tree. Organize that tree around domain or application data, divide it into slices with reducers, and update it only by dispatching actions; component-local values can remain outside Redux.

example.title: One store with a domain slice
example.explanation: Creates one store whose root state has a domain-oriented `todos` slice, then updates it by dispatching an action.

useCases.title: Centralized state inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspecting and debugging shared state

useCases.title: Serialization and hydration
useCases.scenario: Saving and restoring application state

useCases.title: Undo and redo
useCases.scenario: Reverting a sequence of updates

useCases.title: Domain-oriented state organization
useCases.scenario: Sharing related data across features

interview.question: What does “single state tree” mean in Redux?
interview.answer: Redux stores the application’s global state as one object tree inside one store. This creates a single source of truth that can be inspected, serialized, hydrated, and persisted.
interview.followUp: Why can a Redux app still have multiple reducers? Reducers can be composed to manage separate parts of the same state tree while the application retains one store.

interview.question: How should the single state tree be structured?
interview.answer: The tree should be organized around domain data and application state, with top-level keys commonly representing related slices. It should not mirror the component hierarchy.
interview.followUp: How should related entities be represented? Prefer normalized data: store each object once by ID and let references store IDs rather than duplicated objects.

interview.question: How is the single state tree updated?
interview.answer: State changes happen by dispatching plain-object actions. Pure reducers receive the previous state and an action, then return the next state without mutating the previous state.
interview.followUp: How can update logic scale? Combine smaller reducers, each responsible for a particular portion of the state tree, into the root reducer.

keyPoints: Redux represents shared application state as one tree held by one store.
Centralized state supports straightforward debugging and inspection.
The tree can be persisted during development to speed up iteration.
Whole-tree history makes features such as undo and redo easier to implement.
gotchas: Do not create separate stores for different domains; combine reducers into one root reducer and keep one store.
Views and callbacks must not write directly to the state; dispatch actions instead.
A single tree does not require one giant reducer; split reducer logic as the application grows.

Redux data modeling::Event-style actions.summary: Model actions as events that describe what happened, rather than as setters for individual state fields. This produces clearer names, fewer dispatches, and more useful Redux DevTools history.
Redux data modeling::Event-style actions.explanation: Model actions as descriptions of events that occurred, such as an order being placed, rather than commands that directly set individual state fields. The action type communicates what happened, while the payload carries the additional facts reducers need to calculate the state update.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: A plain JavaScript object with a required `type` field; additional event data is conventionally stored in `payload`.

parameters.name: action.type
parameters.description: A readable string commonly formatted as `domain/eventName`, identifying the event.

parameters.name: action.payload
parameters.description: Optional additional information describing the event; it may be a number, string, object, array, or another value.

Redux data modeling::Event-style actions.returns: No return value is specified for the modeling guideline; dispatching an action causes reducers to calculate updated state.

example.title: Model an action as an event
example.explanation: Dispatches one meaningful event describing an order, rather than separate setters for each resulting field.

useCases.title: Represent one business occurrence
useCases.scenario: A user completes a multi-field interaction and the resulting state changes belong to one business event.

useCases.title: Coordinate related updates
useCases.scenario: Several state fields change because one action occurred.

useCases.title: Improve DevTools history
useCases.scenario: Teams need an action log that explains application behavior during debugging.

useCases.title: Reduce setter proliferation
useCases.scenario: A feature has many possible state fields but should avoid one action type per field.

interview.question: What distinguishes an event-style action from a setter?
interview.answer: An event-style action describes something that happened in the application, while a setter tells Redux to assign a particular field value. Event-style modeling usually produces more meaningful names, fewer dispatches, and a clearer DevTools history.
interview.followUp: Why can one event replace several setters? A single event can carry the facts needed by a reducer, which then determines the resulting changes to state.

interview.question: How should event-style action types and data be structured?
interview.answer: Use a readable type string, commonly shaped as `domain/eventName`, and choose a name that communicates the occurrence. Put additional information needed to describe the event in `payload`.
interview.followUp: What makes a payload design useful? It should contain the information the reducer needs to respond to the event without turning the action type into an implementation detail.

interview.question: Why do action names matter beyond reducer matching?
interview.answer: Action types are inspected by reducers to decide whether to handle an action, and they appear in the Redux DevTools history. Descriptive event names therefore help both update logic and debugging.
interview.followUp: Why avoid `SET_DATA`? It does not reveal what occurred, so the action history provides little useful information about application behavior.

keyPoints: Name actions after meaningful occurrences instead of exposing implementation-level field assignments.
Event-oriented names make the action log easier to read and communicate application behavior.
Event modeling can reduce dispatch noise and improve the usefulness of recorded Redux history.
An event tells the application what happened and leaves the reducer to determine how state should respond.
Choose action types that clearly summarize the application occurrence they represent.
A useful action history should communicate what happened without requiring inspection of every payload.
gotchas: Generic setter-like names hide the event and make the action history difficult to understand.
Creating one setter action per field can produce excessive action types and dispatches.
Redux does not enforce event wording, so meaningful action design remains the application's responsibility.

Redux data modeling::Local versus global.summary: Keep isolated or non-critical UI details in component state. Prefer Redux for shared data or values that benefit from reuse, derivation, caching, time-travel debugging, or consistency across hot reloads.
Redux data modeling::Local versus global.explanation: Choose ownership by asking who needs the data and what capabilities it must support. Put shared, reusable, cacheable, derivable, time-travel-debuggable, or hot-reload-consistent data in Redux; keep isolated UI details in component state.

example.title: Shared data in Redux, form state locally
example.explanation: The posts collection belongs in Redux because it is shared application data, while the form draft remains component state because only the form uses it.

useCases.title: Local form state
useCases.scenario: A form's draft fields are used only by that form.

useCases.title: Shared application data
useCases.scenario: Several screens need the same fetched records.

useCases.title: Normalized relational data
useCases.scenario: Entities have IDs and relationships.

useCases.title: Cached data
useCases.scenario: Previously fetched values should be reused.

interview.question: When should state be global Redux state rather than local component state?
interview.answer: Redux should hold data that other parts of the application need, especially when multiple components use it or when the app benefits from caching, derived data, time-travel debugging, or consistency during hot reload. State used in only one place can remain local.
interview.followUp: How would you decide where a dropdown's open flag belongs? Usually component state, unless other application areas need to observe or control that flag.

interview.question: Is it wrong to keep UI state outside Redux?
interview.answer: There is no universal rule that every value belongs in Redux. Choose a practical balance based on the application's needs, keeping isolated or non-critical UI state local and shared application data in the store.
interview.followUp: What is a useful test for ownership? Ask whether another part of the application cares about the value or whether multiple components use it.

interview.question: How should relational data be modeled in Redux?
interview.answer: Store related data in a normalized form when it has identifiers, nesting, or relationships: keep each object once by ID, and let references store IDs instead of duplicated objects. Redux Toolkit's createEntityAdapter is recommended for normalized collections in slices.
interview.followUp: Why avoid duplicated entities? Updating one canonical copy prevents inconsistent representations across the application.

keyPoints: Start by checking whether another feature needs the value; cross-feature interest is evidence that Redux ownership may be appropriate.
Data consumed by several components is a strong candidate for the Redux store rather than one component's local state.
Prefer Redux when keeping the source data enables meaningful derived values elsewhere in the application.
State that benefits from restoring historical values can justify global ownership because Redux supports time-travel-oriented workflows.
Caching needs favor Redux when multiple parts of the app should reuse already-fetched data.
Redux is useful when data must survive UI component replacement during hot reload.
gotchas: Do not move isolated UI state into Redux merely for uniformity; when the rest of the application does not use it, component state is usually the better home.
Avoid putting non-serializable values in Redux state unless there is a compelling, deliberate reason.

Redux data modeling::Memoized selectors.summary: Memoized selectors cache derived results and reuse them when selector inputs are unchanged. Redux commonly uses Reselect’s `createSelector` to keep expensive calculations and result references stable.
Redux data modeling::Memoized selectors.explanation: A memoized selector combines input selectors with a result function. It remembers prior arguments and input results, rerunning the derivation only when relevant values differ by reference; otherwise it returns the cached result, preserving referential stability.

parameters.name: inputSelectors
parameters.type: Array of selector functions or separate selector-function arguments
parameters.description: One or more selectors that receive the selector arguments and provide values for the derivation.

parameters.name: resultFunc
parameters.description: The function that receives the input-selector results and computes the derived value.

Redux data modeling::Memoized selectors.returns: A memoized selector function that returns the derived result and reuses the cached result when its inputs are unchanged.

example.title: Memoize a derived todo list
example.explanation: The selector filters completed todos once for unchanged input references and returns the cached array on the repeated call.

useCases.title: Expensive derived collections
useCases.scenario: Filtering, sorting, or transforming normalized state into data needed by a view.

useCases.title: Stable result references
useCases.scenario: Returning a newly created object or array only when its source values change.

useCases.title: Composed selectors
useCases.scenario: Combining several state fields into one reusable value for components.

interview.question: How does `createSelector` decide whether to recompute?
interview.answer: `createSelector` receives input selectors and a result function, then returns a memoized selector. It runs the inputs, compares their results with the previous call, and reruns the result function only when an input result changes.
interview.followUp: Why can a selector still run input selectors after every dispatch? The root state argument commonly changes, so Reselect first checks selector arguments and then uses the input-selector results to decide whether the derivation must rerun.

interview.question: When should a selector be memoized?
interview.answer: Memoization is useful when a selector returns a new object or array reference on each call, or when its calculation is expensive. Reusing the cached reference can prevent unnecessary React-Redux updates.
interview.followUp: When is memoization unnecessary? A selector returning an existing primitive or stable state reference usually gains little from caching.

interview.question: Where should memoized selectors be declared?
interview.answer: Use the same memoized selector instance across calls, typically by declaring it outside a component. Recreating it loses the previous cache and prevents effective reuse.
interview.followUp: What if each component instance needs a different cache? Create a selector factory so each instance owns a stable selector, rather than constructing one on every render.

keyPoints: Memoization stores prior inputs and their derived result so repeated calls can reuse work instead of calculating again.
Reselect is the standard Redux ecosystem library for building memoized selectors.
`createSelector` takes input selectors and a result function, producing the memoized selector.
Unchanged input results cause the derivation to be skipped and the previous result reference to be returned.
Caching limits expensive derivation work to calls where relevant inputs differ.
gotchas: Do not memoize every selector automatically: prioritize selectors that create new object or array references, or perform expensive calculations.
Input selectors must return stable references when their underlying data is unchanged, or the result function will run again.

Redux data modeling::Normalized state.summary: Normalized state stores each entity once in an ID-keyed table and represents relationships with IDs. Separate ID arrays preserve ordering, while Redux Toolkit can provide a standard normalized shape.
Redux data modeling::Normalized state.explanation: Normalized Redux state models each entity type as an ID-keyed lookup table. Relationships store IDs rather than embedded copies, and separate ID arrays can preserve ordering when needed.

example.title: Normalized entity tables
example.explanation: Users and posts are stored once in ID-keyed tables, while a post points to its author through authorId.

useCases.title: Model relationships without duplication
useCases.scenario: Relational application data such as users, posts, comments, or products with references between records.

useCases.title: Enable predictable item access
useCases.scenario: Collections that need frequent direct reads or targeted updates by entity ID.

useCases.title: Represent relationships with join tables
useCases.scenario: Many-to-many relationships or relationships that carry their own attributes.

interview.question: What is normalized state in Redux?
interview.answer: Normalization stores one copy of each entity in a lookup table keyed by its ID. Other records refer to that entity by ID, which avoids duplicated nested data and supports direct lookup.
interview.followUp: How should many-to-many relationships be represented? Use an intermediate join table containing the IDs of the related entities, especially when the relationship has its own data.

interview.question: How would you design a normalized state shape?
interview.answer: Give each data type its own table, store entities as object values keyed by their IDs, and use IDs for references. Use arrays of IDs when the application must represent ordering.
interview.followUp: What standard Redux Toolkit shape supports this pattern? createEntityAdapter uses `{ ids: [], entities: {} }` and supplies reducers and selectors for the collection.

interview.question: What benefits does normalization provide?
interview.answer: Normalization makes item retrieval and updates more consistent because a record can be found directly through its ID. It also ensures that changes to an entity do not require synchronizing duplicated nested copies.
interview.followUp: What should happen when an API returns deeply nested relational data? Transform it into normalized tables before adding it to the store; Normalizr is one option for complex schemas.

keyPoints: Separate entity types into independent state tables, such as users, posts, and comments.
Represent each table as an object whose keys are entity IDs and whose values are the complete entities.
Store relationships as IDs instead of embedding the referenced object again.
Use an ID array alongside the lookup table when a collection needs an explicit sequence.
Treat relational or nested store data like database tables rather than deeply nested duplicated records.
ID-based access makes individual entity reads and writes predictable across slices.
Redux Toolkit can generate the conventional IDs-and-entities structure for normalized collections.
gotchas: An ID-keyed object alone does not express list order, so keep a separate ID array when ordering matters.

Redux data modeling::Selectors.summary: Selectors hide Redux state structure behind reusable functions and derive values from minimal source state. They can also improve performance by memoizing expensive calculations.
Redux data modeling::Selectors.explanation: A selector is a function that receives all or part of Redux state and returns data based on it. Use selectors to hide state-access details, calculate values such as filtered lists, and avoid storing redundant derived data; memoize expensive derivations when repeated recalculation matters.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The Redux store state, or the relevant part of it, from which the selector reads or derives data.

Redux data modeling::Selectors.returns: Data based on the supplied state, either a stored value or a newly derived value.

example.title: Basic selectors
example.explanation: The selectors hide the state layout from callers and derive a filtered list without storing that duplicate data.

useCases.title: Read state through a stable access API
useCases.scenario: A component needs one field or nested value without depending directly on the store's layout.

useCases.title: Derive presentation data
useCases.scenario: A UI needs a filtered, sorted, counted, or aggregated view of stored data.

useCases.title: Share data-selection logic
useCases.scenario: Several components need the same state lookup or calculation.

useCases.title: Memoize expensive derivations
useCases.scenario: A calculation is repeated and should reuse its previous result when inputs are unchanged.

interview.question: What is a selector?
interview.answer: A selector is a function that accepts the Redux state, or part of it, and returns data based on that state. It may simply read a stored value or compute a derived result.
interview.followUp: Why keep derived values out of Redux state? Keeping only source data avoids duplicated state and reduces synchronization problems; compute the result when needed.

interview.question: How do selectors encapsulate state shape?
interview.answer: Selectors centralize knowledge of the state layout and provide reusable access or derivation logic. If the state shape changes, callers can continue using the selector while its implementation is updated.
interview.followUp: Where should reusable selectors live? A slice file is a practical location, because the selector can remain near the state structure it knows about.

interview.question: When should a selector be memoized?
interview.answer: Memoized selectors cache derived results and recalculate only when their inputs change. Reselect's createSelector is the documented Redux ecosystem API for building them.
interview.followUp: What should a selector return when used with useSelector? Prefer a stable reference when the underlying selected data has not changed, otherwise reference comparison may trigger a re-render.

keyPoints: Store the smallest useful source state; calculate additional values with selectors instead of persisting duplicate derived data.
Selectors receive state, or a state subsection, and return a value computed from it.
Selectors provide one place for state lookup and derivation logic, so components do not need to know the store's internal layout.
gotchas: A selector that creates a new result object or array on every call can cause unnecessary React-Redux updates; use memoization for derived results when appropriate.

Redux data modeling::State machines.summary: Represent a workflow with one explicit finite status, such as `idle`, `loading`, `success`, or `failure`, rather than contradictory booleans. Reducers use the current status and action together to allow valid transitions and make impossible states impossible.
Redux data modeling::State machines.explanation: Model a finite workflow with an explicit status value such as `idle`, `loading`, `succeeded`, or `failed`. The reducer uses both the current status and the dispatched action to decide whether a transition is valid, preventing contradictory combinations such as simultaneous loading and failure flags.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The current finite workflow state and associated data.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: An object describing the event that may cause a transition.

Redux data modeling::State machines.returns: A new state value calculated from the current state and dispatched action.

related: Reducers Should Own the State Shape
keyPoints: Use a finite state machine when a workflow must occupy exactly one state from a known set.
Represent mutually exclusive conditions with a single finite-state field instead of several potentially contradictory flags.
A request commonly begins in `idle`, then moves through loading, success, or failure.
The `loading` state explicitly indicates that the operation is currently in progress.
A `success` state records that the operation completed and produced usable data.
A `failure` state records an unsuccessful operation and can be paired with error details.
Reducers should validate transitions using both current state and action, not just the action type.
gotchas: Do not represent mutually exclusive workflow states with independent booleans; use one finite status value so impossible combinations cannot occur.
A transition should consider the current state as well as the action, rather than handling every action unconditionally.
